questions.stem: When facing an NP-hard problem, the three classical coping options are:
questions.explanation: Give up optimality, polynomial time, or generality. Week 11 explores the last option in depth.

questions.stem: Unweighted IS on a tree can be solved by which technique?
choices: Greedy: include leaves, delete them and their parents, recurse
questions.explanation: Exchange argument: there is always a max IS containing every leaf. Greedy O(n).

questions.stem: Why does the leaf-greedy fail for WEIGHTED IS on trees?
choices: A heavy non-leaf vertex can outweigh several lighter leaves; the swap argument no longer preserves weight
questions.explanation: Without unit weights the exchange may strictly decrease total weight; need DP.

questions.stem: What is OPT_in(v) in the weighted IS tree DP?
choices: Max IS weight in subtree rooted at v, including v
Number of vertices in v's subtree
Max IS weight in subtree rooted at v, excluding v
Sum of weights in v's subtree
questions.explanation: OPT_in(v) commits to v being selected, so all v's children must be excluded.

questions.stem: What is OPT_out(v) in the weighted IS tree DP?
choices: Max IS weight in subtree rooted at v, excluding v (children free)
questions.explanation: Without v, each child is independently free to be in or out — take the max.

questions.stem: Weighted IS on a tree runs in:
questions.explanation: Post-order traversal computes the DP in O(n) total time.

questions.stem: Which class of graphs admits polynomial Vertex Cover via Konig's theorem?
questions.explanation: Konig's theorem in bipartite graphs equates max matching with min vertex cover, both polynomial.

questions.stem: An FPT algorithm has running time of the form:
questions.explanation: Fixed-Parameter Tractable separates the exponential dependence from n: f(k) can be huge, but poly(n) keeps it tractable when k is small.

questions.stem: Vertex Cover has an FPT algorithm of what running time?
questions.explanation: Branch on any uncovered edge: try each endpoint in the cover (k decreases by 1); depth k tree, leaves at depth 0; total O(2^k * n).

questions.stem: Which problem is NOT a candidate for tree-DP coping?
questions.explanation: TSP on general graphs is NP-hard; tree DP applies only when input is a tree. The others have polynomial tree DP.

questions.stem: Bounded treewidth gives polynomial-time algorithms because:
choices: DP on the tree decomposition has work f(k) * poly(n) where k is the width
questions.explanation: Tree decompositions yield DP on a tree-like structure; many NP-hard problems become polynomial when k is constant.

questions.stem: Which is NOT a standard exact exponential approach for hard problems?
questions.explanation: Greedy approximation gives up optimality, not polynomial time. The others are exact approaches (though may take exponential time).

questions.stem: When is restricting to trees a useful coping strategy?
choices: When the input is guaranteed to be tree-structured (file systems, parse trees, phylogenetic trees, dependency graphs)
questions.explanation: Many real-world graphs are tree-structured; exploiting that lets you bypass general-graph NP-hardness.

questions.stem: Why does the recurrence OPT_in(v) = w(v) + Sum OPT_out(c) over children c look the way it does?
choices: Children may be either in or out
Including v forbids including any child (adjacent in the tree), so children must use OPT_out
questions.explanation: v in S excludes v's neighbours (its children in the rooted tree). Hence each child contributes its OPT_out value.

questions.stem: What is the base case of the weighted IS tree DP?
questions.explanation: A leaf has no children; including it gives w(leaf), excluding gives 0.

questions.stem: Which restricted class makes 3-COLOURING polynomial?
questions.explanation: Bipartite graphs are 2-colourable; hence trivially 3-colourable. Planar 3-COLOURING is still NP-hard.

questions.stem: Which best describes 'branch-and-bound'?
choices: Systematic search that prunes via upper/lower bounds
questions.explanation: Branch-and-bound explores the solution tree; pruning at nodes whose best-case bound is worse than the current incumbent makes it practical on many instances.

questions.stem: FPT in parameter k differs from XP because:
choices: FPT separates k's exponential cost from n; XP allows n^k (parameter in the exponent of n)
questions.explanation: FPT: f(k) * poly(n). XP: poly(n) with k in the exponent. FPT is much faster in n for fixed k.

questions.stem: Which is the right evaluation order for the tree DP?
questions.explanation: Post-order ensures every child's in/out is available before computing the parent.

questions.stem: If a problem is NP-hard, you can always:
choices: Solve it in O(n log n) on average
Use approximation, restricted inputs, or exact exponential algorithms to mitigate (depending on the problem)
questions.explanation: NP-hardness eliminates only one option (polynomial exact algorithm on general inputs). The other three coping strategies remain.

questions.stem: Planar 3-COLOURING is:
choices: NP-hard, despite the input being planar
questions.explanation: Planarity does not always help — 3-COLOURING stays NP-hard on planar graphs (despite 4-colourability).

questions.stem: Which is the size of an optimal IS in the worked tree example (A-B, A-C, B-D, B-E with weights 5, 4, 2, 3, 3)?
questions.explanation: Select A, D, E giving 5 + 3 + 3 = 11. Bigger than excluding A (gives at most 4 + 2 = 6 from B + C, no — actually 6 + 2 = 8 from out(B) + in(C)).

questions.stem: Which is NOT a 'restricted-instance' algorithmic class mentioned in Week 11?
questions.explanation: Sparse arrays is not a graph class. Trees, bipartite, planar, and bounded-treewidth are the standard restricted classes.

questions.stem: If a problem has a kernel of size poly(k), what does this imply for FPT?
choices: It is FPT because once kernelised to poly(k) size, any algorithm finishes in f(k) time
questions.explanation: Kernelisation reduces the instance to size depending only on k; brute force on the kernel then gives FPT runtime.

questions.stem: Which tradeoff does the W12 'approximation algorithms' topic give up that W11 'restricted instances' does NOT?
questions.explanation: Approximation gives up optimality (returns within factor c); restricted instances keep optimality but limit inputs.
